input: This pricing case considers a SaaS tier and asks, in essence, how much volume the tier needs to sell in order to cover its costs. The tier is priced at $239 per unit, while the variable cost associated with each unit comes to $166 per unit. In addition, the business carries fixed costs of $248k per year, which have to be met regardless of how many units are sold. Bringing these figures together, the break-even volume works out at 3397 units per year, the level of sales at which the total contribution from the units sold exactly matches the fixed costs. Encouragingly, the current volume stands at 7966 units per year, which is comfortably above the break-even level and suggests that the tier is operating with a reasonable margin of safety. Two caveats should nevertheless be kept in mind when interpreting these numbers. The volume figures are last year's actuals, and as such they describe how the tier actually performed in the past rather than how it is guaranteed to perform in the future. Furthermore, the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, which means that the analysis is silent on the question of how demand would respond if the price were to be changed in either direction.
target: Break-even volume for the SaaS tier is 3397 units per year. The price is $239 per unit and the variable cost is $166 per unit, so each unit sold contributes the difference between the two toward the fixed costs of $248k per year; the break-even volume is the fixed costs divided by that contribution. The contribution is stated per unit and the fixed costs per year, which is why the break-even figure carries units of volume per year rather than revenue. Current volume is 7966 units per year, more than double the break-even volume. The tier covers its fixed costs at the current price with room to spare, and a fall in volume could be absorbed down to the break-even point before the tier moved into loss. Two qualifications bound that statement. The volume figures are last year's actuals: they describe the tier as it sold, at the price then charged, and not necessarily as it will sell. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, so the appraisal cannot say whether a price change would raise or lower the contribution the tier earns. A price rise increases the contribution per unit and reduces the break-even volume arithmetically, but it may also reduce the volume itself, and the second effect is the one the figures do not measure. The break-even statement is a yearly statement: it sets the year's contribution against the year's fixed costs and says nothing about the timing of sales within the year.
